VTEMajors2026. Enoxaparin and unfractionated heparin prophylaxis.

Study population and baseline characteristics

The analysis included 712 records with distinct study identifiers, comprising 486 enoxaparin records and 226 UFH records. Recorded weight ranged from 120 to 382 kg, and age ranged from 18 to 97 years.

Median age was 52.0 (41.0 to 62.0) years with enoxaparin and 53.0 (42.0 to 63.0) years with UFH. Median weight was 144.5 (IQR 132.0 to 165.0) kg and 134.9 (IQR 125.2 to 151.0) kg, respectively. Median recorded eGFR was 88.0 (IQR 68.0 to 90.0) with enoxaparin and 80.0 (IQR 54.0 to 90.0) with UFH.

Cancer was recorded in 50 (10.3%) of the enoxaparin group and 54 (23.9%) of the UFH group. Surgery before or at prophylaxis initiation was recorded in 86 (17.7%) and 65 (28.8%), respectively.

Treatment and admission characteristics

Median prophylaxis duration was 5.0 (IQR 3.0 to 9.0) days with enoxaparin and 6.5 (IQR 4.0 to 11.0) days with UFH. A positive missed-dose entry was recorded in 233 (47.9%) and 195 (86.3%), respectively. Weight-based prescribing was flagged in 19 records, all in the enoxaparin group.

VTE, recorded bleeding and haemoglobin drop

VTE occurred in 4/486 enoxaparin records (0.8%) and 13/226 UFH records (5.8%). The risk difference was -4.93 percentage points (95% CI -8.80 to -2.25), and the risk ratio was 0.14 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.43). Fisher exact p <0.001.

Recorded bleed occurred in 9/486 enoxaparin records (1.9%) and 6/226 UFH records (2.7%). The risk difference was -0.80 percentage points (95% CI -3.94 to 1.37), and the risk ratio was 0.70 (95% CI 0.25 to 1.94). Fisher exact p = 0.576.

Haemoglobin drop occurred in 15/486 enoxaparin records (3.1%) and 28/226 UFH records (12.4%). The risk difference was -9.30 percentage points (95% CI -14.38 to -5.14), and the risk ratio was 0.25 (95% CI 0.14 to 0.46). Fisher exact p <0.001.

Time to VTE during prophylaxis

All 712 records contributed usable follow-up, with 17 VTE events over 8,510 prophylaxis-days. Enoxaparin contributed 5988 days and UFH contributed 2522 days. Follow-up began at prophylaxis initiation and ended at VTE or prophylaxis cessation.

The unadjusted enoxaparin-versus-UFH hazard ratio was 0.162 (95% CI 0.053 to 0.500), p = 0.002. The log-rank comparison gave p <0.001.

At day 30, 29 enoxaparin and 14 UFH records remained at risk. The last VTE occurred at day 85, when only 3 UFH records remained at risk. Full follow-up estimates and sensitivity analyses are provided in the appendix.

Curves use the full recorded follow-up, displayed to day 30. Dashed lines are pointwise 95% confidence intervals and crosses denote censoring. These estimates apply to the observed prophylaxis course. Death and other cessation reasons were unavailable, so independent censoring cannot be verified and competing-risk incidence was not estimated.

Adjusted VTE comparisons

Adjustment for cancer and surgery yielded a hazard ratio of 0.161 (95% CI 0.051 to 0.505), p = 0.002. Adding continuous age and sex gave a hazard ratio of 0.198 (95% CI 0.063 to 0.621), p = 0.006. All models included the same 712 records and 17 events.

Drug + cancer + surgeryCancer, yes versus no0.889 (0.247 to 3.191)0.856

Adding cancer and surgery changed the drug HR from 0.162 to 0.161. Adding smoking to this core model changed it to 0.179. The cancer and surgery coefficients were close to one, while current and former smoking had estimates above two relative to never smoking. All four covariate confidence intervals included one and were wide. These data do not precisely establish their individual associations with VTE, or exclude clinically important effects.

The drug estimate changed little after adjustment for these measured covariates. Residual confounding remains possible despite the stability of the adjusted estimates.

The core model estimated three coefficients and the age-and-sex model estimated five. Only 1 VTE event occurred in a female record. The global proportional-hazards diagnostic gave p = 0.097 for the core model and p = 0.009 for the age-and-sex model. Surgery-specific diagnostic p values were 0.050 and 0.001, respectively. The expanded model is therefore presented as exploratory.

Covariate-adjusted analyses were exploratory. Cancer and surgery before or at prophylaxis initiation were included to assess potential baseline confounding. Age and sex, smoking status and baseline renal function were evaluated in separate sensitivity models to limit model complexity given the small number of events. These models do not establish a causal treatment effect.

Smoking sensitivity analysis

Smoking data were available for all 712 records included in the sensitivity analysis. Adding smoking status to the cancer-and-surgery model yielded an enoxaparin-versus-UFH HR of 0.179 (95% CI 0.056 to 0.571, p = 0.004), compared with 0.161 (95% CI 0.051 to 0.505) in the same-cohort model without smoking. The Firth estimate after smoking adjustment was 0.196 (95% CI 0.058 to 0.557).

The smoking-adjusted model's global proportional-hazards test gave p = 0.315. The corresponding smoking-factor test gave p = 0.380, and surgery gave p = 0.117. No convergence warnings were recorded. The model remains limited by sparse events and possible residual confounding. These diagnostic tests have limited power with few events. Firth estimation does not resolve non-proportional hazards or informative cessation.

Smoking was included as a baseline three-level factor: never (N, reference), current (Y) and former (X). Smoking status was added to the cancer-and-surgery model. Age and sex were evaluated in a separate model to limit the number of coefficients relative to the available events.

Baseline renal-function sensitivity analysis

Baseline eGFR was available for 711 adults. eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 was recorded in 9/486 enoxaparin records (1.9%) and 26/226 UFH records (11.5%). Renal-function adjustment assessed potential confounding associated with this baseline imbalance.

On the same complete-case cohort, adding eGFR below 30 to cancer and surgery changed the enoxaparin-versus-UFH HR from 0.161 (95% CI 0.051 to 0.506) to 0.152 (95% CI 0.048 to 0.481). There was only 1 VTE event among 35 adults with eGFR below 30. The renal-category HR was 0.495 (95% CI 0.063 to 3.883). Its wide interval does not support a protective interpretation of lower eGFR.

The exploratory renal sensitivity analysis added one binary baseline covariate to the cancer-and-surgery model and excluded one record with missing eGFR. Smoking, age and sex were evaluated in separate models to limit model complexity. Sparse events, model assumptions and residual confounding limit interpretation.

Exploratory dose comparisons within each drug

For Enoxaparin, the comparison of 80 versus 40 mg/day included 391 of 486 records. There were 0 VTE events over 3681 prophylaxis-days at the higher total and 2 over 863 days at the lower total. The unadjusted rate ratio was 0.000 (95% CI 0.000 to 1.248, exact p = 0.072, Holm-adjusted p = 0.433).

For UFH, the comparison of 15000 versus 10000 units/day included 221 of 226 records. There were 11 VTE events over 1918 prophylaxis-days at the higher total and 2 over 590 days at the lower total. The unadjusted rate ratio was 1.692 (95% CI 0.369 to 15.708, exact p = 0.758, Holm-adjusted p = 1.000).

The 80-versus-40 mg/day enoxaparin comparison included 2 of 4 enoxaparin VTE events. A further exploratory comparison pooled all higher recorded daily totals to include all enoxaparin events. The UFH dose comparison was adjusted for body weight.

ModelMethodRecordsEventsHazard ratio (95% CI)P value
UFH dose onlyCox, Efron221131.277 (0.275 to 5.923)0.755
UFH dose and weightCox, Efron221131.597 (0.334 to 7.636)0.558
UFH dose and weightFirth Cox, Breslow221131.291 (0.350 to 6.935)0.721

The weight-adjusted Cox sensitivity gave a HR of 1.597 (95% CI 0.334 to 7.636), p = 0.558. These intervals remain compatible with clinically important differences in either direction. No equivalence margin or equivalence test was specified, so the results do not establish equal effectiveness of the UFH doses.

The Poisson model uses each adult's VTE indicator and log prophylaxis-days as an offset. It assumes a log-linear weight association and a constant baseline event rate over follow-up. For a first-event endpoint this is an exponential survival model. The Cox sensitivity uses event timing and allows the baseline hazard to vary, while assuming proportional hazards. Both depend on appropriate censoring and adequate control of confounding. Weight adjustment alone does not address all possible reasons for dose selection.

Dose categories are recorded daily totals. Administration frequency, baseline regimen, changes during therapy, renal dose adjustments and time at each regimen were unavailable. Prophylaxis-days are attributed to the recorded total for these exploratory summaries. The descriptive and exact dose comparisons are unadjusted and can reflect differences in patient selection, duration or dose recording. A zero event count gives a boundary rate-ratio estimate and does not establish a protective effect. Bleeding and Hb-drop comparisons use recorded outcome flags, with the timing limitations described in the data checks. The UFH regression models adjusted for weight only. Dose analyses remain exploratory because events are sparse and regimen information is incomplete.

Statistical and data-quality appendices

Distribution assessment and normality tests

Distribution checks comprised histograms, normal Q-Q plots and Shapiro-Wilk tests within each drug group. Shapiro-Wilk p values were below 0.05 for 9 of 10 baseline variable-by-group distributions and 4 of 4 therapy-duration and length-of-stay distributions (13 of 14 overall). Continuous characteristics are summarised using medians and interquartile ranges, with Wilcoxon rank-sum comparisons. Distribution plots and clinical measurement scales informed the summary measures alongside the test results. Wilcoxon comparisons assess rank distributions and do not, in general, test a difference in medians alone. Mean, standard deviation, range, missingness and sample skewness are provided in the descriptive appendix. These diagnostic p values are unadjusted and are not study-outcome hypothesis tests.

Data checks, missingness and event timing
CheckFinding
Records and IDs712 records with 712 distinct study IDs. Repeated admissions cannot be assessed from this ID alone.
Matching record profiles4 records have an identical profile to another record across every non-ID source field, representing 2 additional matching records. All records were retained because duplicate identity could not be established.
Age eligibility713 source records. 1 record aged below 18 years was excluded. All 712 analysed records are adults aged 18 or older.
Drug assignment486 enoxaparin and 226 UFH. Every record has exactly one recorded drug.
Numerical age categories25 age >60 flags disagree with age. 0 age >=70 flags disagree. Categories in Table 1 use numerical age.
Missing eGFR1 record has missing eGFR after treating Nill as unavailable.
Missing BMI and height1 BMI and 1 height values are missing. Summaries use observed values.
Missed-dose scale335 values lie between 0 and 1 and 93 exceed 1. The split follows record-ID batches. Quantitative adherence rates were not estimated because the recording scale was inconsistent. Any positive recorded value is summarised.
Therapy duration and LOS15 therapy durations exceed LOS, each by 1 day. The counting convention was unavailable. A sensitivity analysis excluded these records.
Hb drop timing12 of 43 Hb events lack timing and 2 occur after recorded therapy duration. All event flags are retained.
eGFR upper value311 of 711 numeric eGFR values equal 90. eGFR was recorded before prophylaxis initiation in mL/min/1.73 m2. The reporting convention for values at or above 90 was unavailable.
BMI and dose/weight checks0 BMI, 0 enoxaparin dose/weight and 0 UFH dose/weight discrepancies beyond rounding tolerance.
Variable definitions and record independenceSmoking categories were never (N), current (Y) and former (X). Definitions of IBS, bleeding and haemoglobin drop, administration frequency, treatment switches, and whether each record represented a distinct patient or admission were unavailable.

One record aged 17 years was excluded from every analysis. All remaining adult records were retained in the main analyses. Age categories were derived from numeric age. Non-events have structurally missing event times. Hb-drop events with missing timing remain in the outcome counts. Information on repeated admissions, treatment switches, prophylaxis gaps, death and reasons for cessation was unavailable. Records were analysed as independent observations.

Statistical methods

Continuous summaries use R type 7 quartiles. Normality was assessed with Shapiro-Wilk tests and histogram/Q-Q plots within each treatment group. Wilcoxon tests use the normal approximation with continuity correction. Categorical tests use Pearson chi-square without continuity correction when all expected counts are at least five, otherwise Fisher exact. All tests are two-sided. No automatic variable selection was used.

Between-drug risk differences use Newcombe intervals combining Wilson scores. Risk-ratio intervals use the log-Wald method without continuity correction. Kaplan-Meier intervals use log-log transformation. Cox models use Efron ties and Wald intervals unless stated otherwise. The cancer-and-surgery, age-and-sex and smoking models used the same complete cohort. Covariate-adjusted and dose analyses were post hoc and are interpreted as exploratory.

Smoking was entered as a baseline three-level factor: never (N, reference), current (Y) and former (X). The smoking model included drug, cancer and baseline surgery and estimated five coefficients from 17 events. Conventional Cox models used Efron ties, with Wald confidence intervals and tests. Firth models used a penalty of 0.5, Breslow ties and profile penalised-likelihood confidence intervals and tests. Conventional Breslow models separate tie-handling differences from penalisation.

Post hoc pairwise dose comparisons used the two most common recorded daily totals within each drug: 80 versus 40 mg/day for enoxaparin and 15,000 versus 10,000 units/day for UFH. Other recorded totals remain in the descriptive tables and were excluded only from these pairwise comparisons. Risk confidence intervals are two-sided Clopper-Pearson intervals. VTE rates use exact Poisson confidence intervals. Rate ratios use conditional equal-tailed exact confidence intervals with central two-sided p values calculated as twice the smaller binomial tail, capped at one. Poisson comparisons assume independent event counts with the specified person-time exposures and a constant rate within each group. Risk differences use Newcombe intervals from Wilson scores without continuity correction. Bleed and Hb-drop risk comparisons use two-sided Fisher exact tests. VTE risk differences are descriptive without a duplicate hypothesis test. The six pairwise dose tests, comprising two VTE rate tests and four bleed or Hb-drop risk tests, are reported with both nominal and Holm-adjusted p values. Confidence intervals are pointwise 95% intervals.

Analyses were performed in R version 4.3.3 using survival 3.5.8 and coxphf 1.13.4.

Methods references: Shapiro-Wilk, exact Poisson intervals, Cox models, proportional-hazards diagnostics, Firth Cox estimation, Newcombe risk differences, and observational comparative-effects methods.
